articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'The Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future' (Digest No.1994/154)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future
IEE Colloquium on Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future
abstract: With 130000 members, the IEE has the largest membership of all the Engineering Institutions in the UK. With 60000 Corporate Members, it can be assumed that more than half of the IEE Membership are in the process of gaining, or aspiring towards, Chartered status. They will do so via the following route: an IEE-accredited BEng engineering degree, at a minimum of second class honours, or equivalent; an IEE-accredited training scheme of at least two years' duration, or equivalent; and at least two years of 'responsible experience'. In addition, applicants are required to undertake a professional review which includes an informal interview of about 45 minutes' duration. This formation process is identified as being appropriate to instill the creative and innovative attributes required of a Chartered Engineer whilst providing the knowledge and understanding of the fundamental principles and analytical skills necessary to solve new engineering problems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Pathways to engineering practice: Incorporated Engineer
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future
abstract: In the United Kingdom, the Engineering Council registers professionally qualified engineering personnel at three levels: Chartered Engineer (CEng), Incorporated Engineer (IEng) and Engineering Technician (EngTech). The IEEIE-the largest Incorporated body, with nearly 30000 members-nominates individuals to the IEng and EngTech registers and is authorised to accredit at both levels. Historically the academic routes to IEng status have been via relevant Higher National Certificates or Diplomas. Since July 1990 the minimum academic qualification for Corporate Membership of the IEEIE has been exemplified by an accredited HND. However, the number of IEEIE members with degrees is increasing, partly reflecting the need for Chartered Electrical Engineers to be in possession of an accredited Honours degree, and also as a result of the current computer-based technological revolution in industry.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: At the cutting edge-the view of practitioners. Chartered Engineer's view
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future
abstract: This paper is concerned with the training needs of current Chartered Engineers and sources personal experience of a recent training programme in line with the requirements of the Institution of Electrical Engineers. It references Pre-University experience, Degree and Company training to date and future expectations, including possible accelerated development programmes and personal training plans. Inadequacies have been identified and solutions outlined. The paper also deals with the present role within the business.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The role and potential of GNVQs
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future
abstract: General National Vocational Qualifications (GNVQs) were introduced in September 1992. GNVQs lie at the very heart of the evolving National Framework of Qualifications. Advanced GNVQs-or 'vocational A Levels'-are the natural successor to the earlier ONC/Ds and the more recent BTEC National Certificates and Diplomas. They are the key to success for the National Framework of Qualifications and to making rapid progress towards meeting National Targets for Education and Training. This paper discusses the Advanced GNVQ in Engineering-a qualification designed to provide opportunities for candidates to develop the skills, knowledge and understanding that underpin the creation of engineered products, engineering systems and services. The Advanced GNVQ in Engineering will also provide opportunities to address wider issues concerned with the value of engineering to society and the environment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Meeting the needs of industry into the next millennium
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future
abstract: A discussion document entitled 'Review of Engineering Formation' was issued in August 1993, and was intended to promote discussion in the following areas: structure and needs of industry; UK education and training system; international comparisons; occupational standards and N/SVQ system; and accountability and quality assessment. The author briefly discusses the contents of the discussion document and then discusses the findings of consultants in respect of future trends. A summary of the keypoints is given. Against this background the author looks at the existing state of affairs, particularly regarding education and marketing.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The role of the Incorporated Engineer-present and future
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future
abstract: There is a particular development path that Incorporated Engineers tend to follow. The majority will have started off as artisans/technicians and will have gained skills, knowledge and expertise over a period of time. They will have also generally taken the ONC/HNC route to qualifications which enables a balance between theory and practical to dictate the model for learning. The Incorporated Engineer has the ability and the confidence to succeed within a given sphere of responsibility. There is also the inherent ability to work successfully at the majority of intellectual levels. Consequently there is a need to firmly establish the role and status of the Incorporated Engineer and gain/enhance full recognition both nationally and internationally of our standing in the world of engineering. Creating an infrastructure which allows for prospective members to be identified early, and then recruited, needs to be a primary objective. Understanding NVQ's and any other innovations in education and training is necessary to ensure that the membership net catches all those potential Incorporated Engineers. At the other end of the scale is the need to continue to promote and provide effective CPD until the loop is closed by new members having moved through a generation lifecycle of membership.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Developing Chartered Engineers-a development managers views
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future
abstract: Surveys of graduates in employment reveal interesting views of their expectations. Most graduates, when asked the question 'What are you looking for out of your training/employment?'-are asking for Career Development. When asked further as to their definition of Career Development, the most frequent meaning is of promotion/hierarchical move. A more realistic definition of Career Development is 'enhancing my personal capability', or 'Continuous Learning'. To achieve this British Aerospace Defence Ltd. have introduced for all staff a Personal Development Review (PDR). It is important to recognise that this generally falls outside the performance assessment and rewards process. People are assessed against achievement of output, not development. Development then underpins and enables performance. The Personal Development Review (PDR), is the start of a continuous coaching and learning process between you and your boss.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Development of standard at National and Scottish vocational qualification (NVQ/SVQ) levels IV and V (moving towards a complementary framework of qualifications)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Roles of Chartered and Incorporated Engineers - Present and Future
abstract: The UK's record of education, training and qualification has been inadequate and the actual needs of employment have not been satisfied. Professional Engineering Institutions are already responding by sharpening their focus on competence, continuing professional development and objective assessment. Although substantial issues remain to be resolved, the NVQ/SVQ concept can provide the tools to deliver this focus. It overlaps and complements historical membership criteria rather than replacing them. The NVQ/SVQ system is well advanced and is being extended. Failure to apply it to higher levels of engineering will encourage division within engineering occupations as a whole. Failure of the profession to take leadership is an opportunity for others bidding for entry into the Institutions' traditional territory.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
